Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: I am permanently an outsider now
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Aleksander Nowak is a 28-year-old Polish-American man who works as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing agency in Chicago. He lives with his long-term partner in a north-side apartment and, to most colleagues who interact with him through scheduled Slack messages and polished content calendars, presents as organised and dependable. He came to his first intake session speaking carefully, in sentences that felt rehearsed - because they were. Before any conversation of consequence, Aleksander runs through likely exchanges in his head, testing words for safety before he commits to them aloud.

He served two tours with a National Guard infantry unit and was medically separated at twenty-six following an incident during his second deployment in which the vehicle he was riding in was struck by an IED on a narrow road outside a forward operating base. The explosion killed one soldier seated beside him and left a second with catastrophic leg injuries. Aleksander was thrown clear of the vehicle but largely uninjured. What he remembers of the minutes that followed does not arrive as a coherent scene. There are pieces: the smell of burning, a hand - he cannot say whose - the sound of a rotary aircraft arriving overhead. The pieces do not connect into a story he can hold. Sometimes the grief and terror of that roadside come over him with full force while he is doing something entirely ordinary, and there is no image attached, no clear memory to point to - only the feeling, arriving without warning like a pressure change in the air. He has said more than once that when he tries to think about what happened, it feels less like remembering something he lived through and more like reading about a stranger's worst day. He had come to believe, quietly and with some shame, that a different man would have been in a different seat, would have reacted faster, would not have walked away while others did not.

In the two years since his separation, a set of habits formed that now shape his daily life in ways that have become difficult to ignore. He drives only when he is alone. Sitting in a passenger seat, or with anyone beside him, produces a physical reaction he cannot override - his chest tightens, his hands press flat against his thighs, and he watches the road with an attention that exhausts him. His partner has largely stopped asking to be driven anywhere, and the two of them have settled into an unspoken arrangement around this that neither has named directly. At his desk, he manages accounts that occasionally require sourcing or moderating news content, and on more than one occasion he has encountered images of injured people in user-generated posts - visible wounds, bloodied limbs - and found himself unable to continue working for the remainder of the afternoon, his body responding as though the image were something happening nearby rather than something on a screen. He routes his content review through filters where possible, and his supervisor believes this is a workflow preference.

Helicopter sounds, common enough over a city, reach him before he consciously registers them. By the time he identifies the source, his pulse is already elevated and he is scanning the room. He sleeps poorly, lying awake with a vigilance that feels necessary to him - he is certain, in those hours, that relaxing his attention would be a mistake. He startles badly when touched without warning, and his partner has learned to announce themselves before entering a room where Aleksander cannot see the door. He avoids anything that places his body under physical stress - he stopped running, avoids crowded transit, and declined an invitation to a gym class a colleague organised. He does not go near anything that resembles a uniform or a weapon, including a police officer standing outside a coffee shop he used to visit regularly.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a single event but an accumulation: his partner said, gently but directly, that they felt they were living with someone who was always waiting for something terrible to happen. Aleksander could not disagree. What he fears most, sitting in the intake chair, is that they are right - that this is simply who he is now, and that the person who existed before that road outside the FOB is not coming back.
